label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

That’s not an exact quote, but it’s close. A few people in the group chat agreed with her, and I can see why. From the outside, this probably looks like a very easy problem to solve: a parent complained about a history project, the principal wants me to drop it, and I could just teach something else.

I’m not going to drop it. I am going to change it.

I wanted to explain why here, partly because I don’t want to have this conversation in fifteen separate texts, but mostly because Jess deserves a better answer than the one I gave her last night, which was something along the lines of “I can’t just cave.” That sounded tougher and simpler than I actually feel.

For the past four years, my two US History II classes at Cobb Street High have done an oral history project on busing and desegregation in Boston from 1974 to 1976. The students are juniors. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood, make a ten-minute recording, and write a two-page reflection.

Until now, I’d never had a complaint about it.

This week, a parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen and copied a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Dr. Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. The three of us are meeting Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I don’t think the parent is being ridiculous. I don’t think she’s trying to erase history, and I’m not interested in picking a fight with her. She has a point about pressure. An assignment can say “family or neighborhood” and still leave a kid feeling like the obvious thing is to go home and ask a grandparent questions they don’t want to answer. It can put a student in the position of hearing something painful about someone they love, then having to decide what to do with it in front of a teacher and classmates.

I should have built a clearer alternative into the project before now. I’m going to add one: students can interview a librarian or archivist, or use recorded interviews from past years, where we have permission. No one should have to interview a family member to complete a history assignment.

But I want to keep the project.

In 2023, a student I’ll call D. interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class, and when it ended nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute.

I remember looking around and realizing they were listening differently than they usually did. Not because I’d found the perfect primary source or delivered a particularly good lesson. His grandmother was a real person, and she was telling them about a place they knew. D. was hearing something new about his own family, and the rest of us were hearing it with him.

Last year, another student found out that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice, and her reflection was the best thing I read all year. I’m proud of the thought she put into it, but I don’t want to make her discomfort sound like a teaching triumph. She had to sit with something hard about someone in her family. That mattered more than the grade or how much I admired her writing.

I keep coming back to the line between asking students to engage with uncomfortable history and forcing them into an uncomfortable situation. I do think the kids who are uncomfortable with this history may be the ones who need to spend time with it most. But that doesn’t give me the right to send them home to question their families, or to make them share something personal with a room full of people. I can ask them to study the history. I need to give them a reasonable choice about how they do it.

And it *is* their history, whether their families were here in the seventies or not. It happened in the city where they live. They know these neighborhoods and these streets. Their textbook gives busing about a paragraph. A paragraph can tell you dates and policies; it can’t do much to show you what those decisions felt like to the people living through them, or how long a story can stay quiet in a family.

Jess knows all of this, by the way. We met student teaching at the same school in 2012. She left teaching in 2019 and works in HR at a biotech in Cambridge now, but she hasn’t forgotten what schools are like. When she tells me to be careful, she’s not saying the assignment doesn’t matter. She’s saying *I* matter, and that I have a job I need to keep.

She’s also not wrong about the risk. I’ve had tenure since 2021, so I’m not pretending I can be fired on a whim for an assignment. But Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP. There are ways for a year at school to get harder that have nothing to do with losing your job. I’m honestly a little scared of the meeting, and I keep rehearsing what I’ll say. I don’t feel especially brave.

What I do feel is that dropping the project altogether would be the wrong response to a concern I can address. The parent has given me a reason to make it better. I want to hear what she has to say on Thursday, tell her about the alternatives, and listen if she thinks I’m still missing something. I hope we can find a way forward without pretending there’s nothing worth discussing.

Jess, I’m not asking you to agree with me. I know you were looking out for me, and I love you for it. I just wanted you to know I’ve thought about what you said—and why, even knowing I could get burned, I’m not ready to let this one go.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting.
